syllabus_version.title: CBSE Curriculum for the Academic Year 2026-27

topics.title: Why Economics? Economic activities and economic agents

concepts.learning_objective: Identify economic activities as those undertaken for monetary gain, the 'ordinary business of life'.
Distinguish consumer, seller, producer, employee and employer by the role a person plays.

topics.title: Scarcity, alternative uses and the problem of choice

concepts.learning_objective: Explain scarcity of resources relative to unlimited wants as the root of all economic problems.
Explain how alternative uses of limited resources give rise to the problem of choice.

topics.title: Consumption, production, distribution and the scope of economics

concepts.learning_objective: Classify an economic question as a study of consumption, production or distribution.
Explain why modern economics includes special studies such as poverty and disparity, which need statistics.

topics.title: Statistics in economics: data, analysis and policies

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise economic facts as economic data needed to analyse economic problems.
Relate the analysis of causes of an economic problem to the formulation of policies.

topics.title: What is statistics? Quantitative and qualitative data

concepts.learning_objective: State the meaning of statistics and the stages of a statistical study.
Distinguish quantitative data from qualitative data (attributes).

topics.title: What statistics does: functions and limits

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how statistics makes facts precise and condenses mass data into summary measures.
Explain the use of statistics in finding economic relationships, predicting trends and framing policy.
Evaluate the misuse of statistical measures and why they are no substitute for common sense.
Explain what a variable, an observation and data are, using the example of food grain production.
State the purpose of collecting data in economics.

topics.title: Sources of data: primary and secondary

concepts.learning_objective: Identify primary data as first-hand information collected by the investigator through an enquiry.
Identify secondary data as data collected and processed by another agency and state its advantages.
Apply the rules for framing good questions: brief, clear, general to specific, no leading or double-negative questions.
Distinguish open-ended questions from closed-ended two-way and multiple-choice questions, with their merits and limits.

topics.title: Modes of data collection and pilot survey

concepts.learning_objective: Compare personal interviews, mailed questionnaires and telephone interviews by their merits and demerits.
Explain the purpose of a pilot survey (pre-testing of the questionnaire).
Describe the census or complete enumeration method and the Indian Census.
Identify the population and a representative sample for a given study and state why sample surveys are preferred.
Explain random sampling, the lottery method and random number tables.
Explain non-random sampling based on judgement, purpose, convenience or quota.
Calculate the sampling error as the difference between a population parameter and its sample estimate.
Identify non-sampling errors (sampling bias, non-response, errors in data acquisition) and explain why they are more serious.
State the main facts about the Census of India as a source of demographic data.
Describe the role of the National Sample Survey and its publication Sarvekshana.

topics.title: Raw data and the need for classification

concepts.learning_objective: Recognise raw data and explain why large raw data are difficult to analyse.
Explain classification as grouping things on the basis of some criteria and state its advantages.
Distinguish chronological (time-based) and spatial (location-based) classification of data.
Classify data on attributes on the basis of the presence or absence of a quality.
Identify quantitative classification of measurable characteristics into classes.
Identify a continuous variable as one that can take any value, including fractions, within a range.
Identify a discrete variable as one that changes only by finite jumps, even when its values are fractions.

topics.title: Frequency distribution: class limits, class interval and class mark

concepts.learning_objective: Identify lower and upper class limits and compute the class interval of a class.
Calculate the class mark of a class and use class marks to draw a frequency curve.
Interpret class frequencies and relative frequencies in a frequency distribution.

topics.title: Number and size of classes; equal and unequal intervals

concepts.learning_objective: Compute the range and relate it to the number of classes and the size of the class interval.
Explain the situations in which unequal class intervals are preferred.

topics.title: Class limits: inclusive and exclusive methods and adjustment

concepts.learning_objective: Distinguish inclusive and exclusive class intervals and place values that equal a class limit.
Adjust inclusive class limits to restore continuity and find adjusted limits and class marks.

topics.title: Tally marking, loss of information, unequal classes and frequency array

concepts.learning_objective: Use tally marks, grouped in fives, to find class frequencies.
Explain the loss of information in grouped data and why unequal classes can make class marks more representative.
Prepare and interpret a frequency array for a discrete variable.
Define a bivariate frequency distribution and read the frequency in a cell of a bivariate table.
Distinguish univariate from bivariate data and interpret row and column totals.

topics.title: Forms of Presentation and Textual Presentation

concepts.learning_objective: Name the three forms of presenting data: textual, tabular and diagrammatic.
Explain when textual presentation is suitable and state its main drawback.
Describe how a table arranges data in rows, columns and cells.
Distinguish qualitative, quantitative, temporal and spatial classification of data.
Identify the table number, title, captions, stubs, body, unit, source and note of a table.
Locate and interpret a figure in the body of a table from its row and column.
Describe the construction and use of a simple bar diagram.
Choose between multiple and component bar diagrams for a given comparison.
Convert component percentages into angles at the centre by multiplying by 3.6 degrees.
Explain when a pie diagram is appropriate and how it relates to a component bar diagram.

topics.title: Histogram, Frequency Polygon and Frequency Curve

concepts.learning_objective: Construct a histogram, using frequency density for unequal class intervals, and read the mode from it.
Distinguish a histogram from a bar diagram.
Describe how a frequency polygon and a frequency curve are drawn and used.
Draw less than and more than ogives and locate the median at their intersection.
Use an arithmetic line graph to study trend in time series data.

topics.title: Need for averages and types of central tendency

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why a large data set is summarised by a single representative value.
Identify the arithmetic mean, median and mode as the common averages and what each conveys.
Compute the arithmetic mean of individual observations by the direct method.
Compute the mean using the assumed mean and step deviation methods.

topics.title: Arithmetic mean of grouped data, its properties and weighted mean

concepts.learning_objective: Compute the mean of discrete and continuous series using frequencies and mid-points.
State that deviations from the mean sum to zero and that the mean is affected by extreme values.
Compute a weighted arithmetic mean when items differ in importance.
Locate the median of individual and discrete series using the (N+1)/2th item.
Compute the median of a continuous series using the median class formula.
Evaluate why the median is not affected by extreme values.
Define and compute the lower and upper quartiles of a series.
Interpret percentiles and relate P50 to the median.
Identify the mode of a discrete series and recognise unimodal and bimodal data.
Compute the mode of a continuous series using the modal class formula.

topics.title: Relative position of mean, median and mode and choice of average

concepts.learning_objective: State that the median lies between the mean and the mode.
Select the most appropriate average for a given purpose and distribution.

topics.title: Meaning of correlation and types of relationship

concepts.learning_objective: Explain that correlation measures covariation between two variables and does not by itself imply cause and effect.
Identify relationships that arise from pure coincidence or from the influence of a third variable.
Classify a relationship between two variables as positive or negative correlation from the direction of their movement.
Interpret the direction and closeness of points in a scatter diagram.
Recognise perfect positive, perfect negative, no correlation and non-linear patterns in scatter diagrams.
Relate the covariance and standard deviations of X and Y to the coefficient of correlation r.
Calculate Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation from deviations about the mean.
Explain why Karl Pearson's r should be used only for a linear relationship.
State that r is a pure number lying between -1 and +1.
Interpret the sign and magnitude of r, including the values 1, -1 and 0.
Apply the property that r is independent of change of origin and scale.
Calculate r using transformed variables U and V in the step deviation method.
Identify situations in which Spearman's rank correlation is preferred to Karl Pearson's coefficient.
Calculate the rank correlation coefficient when ranks are given or worked out from data.
Assign average ranks to repeated values and apply the correction factor.
Explain an index number as a statistical device measuring the average change in a group of related variables.
Interpret index values relative to a base period whose value is set at 100.
Distinguish between price index numbers and quantity index numbers.
Calculate a simple aggregative price index and state its limitations.
Calculate and interpret Laspeyre's price index using base-period quantity weights.
Calculate and interpret Paasche's price index using current-period quantity weights.

topics.title: Construction by the method of averaging relatives

concepts.learning_objective: Compute price relatives and the simple average of price relatives.
Compute a weighted index of price relatives and explain the role of weights.

topics.title: Consumer Price Index and Wholesale Price Index

concepts.learning_objective: Construct and interpret a consumer price index from weights and price relatives.
Describe the coverage, base and uses of the Wholesale Price Index.

topics.title: Index of Industrial Production and Sensex

concepts.learning_objective: Explain how the Index of Industrial Production weights quantity relatives and why its base is revised.
Describe the composition, base and significance of the Sensex.

topics.title: Issues in the construction of an index number

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why the purpose of an index and a representative choice of items matter.
Identify the desirable properties of a base year.
Recognise that the formula and data source must suit the question being studied.
State the uses of CPI, WPI, IIP and Sensex in economic policy.
Calculate the rate of inflation from successive values of a price index.
Calculate the purchasing power of money, real wage and the salary needed to maintain living standards.

topics.title: Introduction: identifying the problem and the target group
topics.ncert_sections: 1; Steps towards making a project (identifying a problem, choice of target group)

concepts.learning_objective: Explain why a project must begin with a clearly identified problem or area of study.
Choose a suitable target group for a project and explain its role in framing questions.

topics.title: Collection of data for a project
topics.ncert_sections: Steps towards making a project (collection of data)

concepts.learning_objective: Decide, from the objective of the survey, whether primary data, secondary data or both are needed.
State the requirements of a postal questionnaire and of a suitable sampling method.

topics.title: Organisation, analysis, conclusion and bibliography
topics.ncert_sections: Steps towards making a project (organisation and presentation, analysis and interpretation, conclusion, bibliography)

concepts.learning_objective: Identify tabulation and diagrams as the tools for organising and presenting collected data.
Select the measure of central tendency, dispersion or correlation suited to a given analytical need.
Describe the role of the conclusion and the bibliography in a project report.
Recognise that a project may take up any topic dealing with an economic issue.
Identify the data needed for a suggested project such as a savings survey or a loan proposal.

topics.title: Sample project: information needs and the questionnaire

concepts.learning_objective: List the information the toothpaste project needs and relate it to the study's objective.
Explain how the questionnaire is designed to generate the required information.

topics.title: Sample project: data analysis, interpretation and concluding note
topics.ncert_sections: 3 (data analysis and interpretation, simplified project report)

concepts.learning_objective: Calculate the mean and standard deviation of a grouped distribution by the step-deviation method.
Interpret the tables of the sample report to draw observations.
Summarise the main findings stated in the concluding note of the sample report.
